messages.subject_clean: Underestimating density?
messages.body_plain:
Michelle, it's impossible to tell what you did do from that
description.  Not sure what you mean by a detection probability of 65 -
do you mean 0.65?  If you pooled data across the 9 visits, then effort
per point should be 9, when you analyse in Distance.  Better to work
with density rather than calculate abundance, but if you do want to
calculate estimated number of birds on your 16 plots, then you would
just multiply density by the plot area:  plot area is16 times pi*50^2
assuming your truncation distance w was 50m.  Make sure you're working
with the right units - I'm guessing 50 here is in metres, but your
density may be numbers per hectare for example.

For your point counts, you can estimate density, assuming you detected
everything on the plots, as total number of birds recorded (number of
detections times mean cluster size) divided by 9 times the area of the
plots, assuming you pooled data from the 9 visits.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Aerial surveys with different types of windows
messages.subject_clean: Aerial surveys with different types of windows
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,I am seeking guidance on my analyses of marine mammal aerial survey
data in Distance 6.0 R2. I have two years worth of data at my disposal and
two types of aircrafts were used : either one fitted with bubble windows or
one fitted with flat windows. It is my understanding that these two types of
platforms will surely give distinct view-fields both on a vertical and a
horizontal axis (as a result for example the blind strip under the plane
will be more or less wide), so I thought it would be legitimate to analyze
the related subsets of my data separately. Is this a good approach ? I want
estimates for each year - should I rather run my analyses on the data pooled
over surveys (i.e regardless of window type) for each year ? Does it depend
on the number of observations closer to the trackline obtained one or the
other type of platform ?
Moreover, the ultimate goal of my work will be to yield daily estimates (by
post-stratifying by day, number of detections per stratum permitting) that
will later be integrated in a migration count model. Following example 8.6
("House wren densities") p 361-366 of Buckland et al. 2001 it seemed to me
that running analyses on an entire dataset using different candidate models
to start with, then choosing the best one and possibly relying on that model
to post stratify was acceptable. Do you agree ? The thing is that I have
(for various motives) 3 right truncation distances (largest observation, 13
km and 5 km) and several left truncation distances (contingent upon the type
of window used) to test. This added to different combination of models +
model selection procedures, I end up with tens (if not more) of analyses to
consider. I fear this might be too much and as a consequence that I might
not be thinking of this all the right way. Any suggestion(s) on how to
proceed ?
Any help, guidance, advice, comments or corrections will be most welcome.
Warm thanks in advance for your input,
Phil

messages.body_plain:
It is possible to handle both platforms simultaneously with different
blind spots but not in the existing code.  Thus I suggest that you left
truncate all the data for the maximum value from the flat windows, pool
all the data and look at platform as a possible covariate for
differences in detection probability using the MCDS engine.

With regard to the migration count, not sure how that fits into the wren
example. Also, you'll need to translate the area you sampled into time
based on average speed of migration to work in the migration idea.
Presumably they are all travelling in the same direction.

--jeff

Your concerns are quite valid.  You are in a bit of a pickle.  The only=20
thing I can suggest is to bound the results by running the analysis as=20

a category of beyond the last bin.  Also, I suggest that you consider=20
having unequal distance bins with increasing bin size with distance --=20
use equal vertical angles.  I suggest reading ch7 thoroughly as there=20
maybe other considerations I've not thought of here.

regards --jeff

messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I'm doing a study of habitat associations of songbirds using point transect
counts. I would like to generate densities of neotropical migratory birds at
the stratum level (by count station, 3 -6 visits per station). For some
reason, DISTANCE allows me to generate densities only by using a global
detection function. It shows numerous unknown error messages and doesnt
complete the analysis when I select detection function to be calculated by
stratum alone. It may be a sample size issue. In any case, my question has
to do with using densities calculated with a global detection function to
run additional (non-DISTANCE) analyses at the stratum level (densities at
each count station). I want to see if and how densities at each count
station differ with respect to two principal components of my habitat
variables. Are there non-independence issues in using densities created from
a detection function of *all count stations* in an analyses that tests for
differences in densities *between count stations*? Does this weaken the
analysis? Is there a better way to proceed? Thank You.

Jared Zimmerman

messages.body_plain:
Jared:

Many of your suspicions are correct.  Fitting a detection function means you are
trying to fit a function to a set of detections; to do a reasonable job of that,
you ought to have ~70 data points to fit that function.  That is why you are
seeing complaints by DISTANCE when you attempt to produce detection functions
for your stations (which I presume are points).

When you use the global detection function to derive your point-specific density
estimates, you do indeed have non-independence issues because estimates for all
of your points share the common detection function and hence are correlated.

So there is no free lunch really, if you wish to make comparisons of density
between points, have sufficient data at each point to make the comparisons
legitimate.

Alex:

I'm not certain I am using terms exactly as you do.  But I interpret
your term 'surveys' as 'transects.'  From that starting point, you
*must* include information about sampling effort you exerted (even if it
did not result in detections) in your analysis.  Very roughly stated,
the estimate of density of birds (simplifying to say all detections are
of groups of size 1) follows this formula (Eqn 2.11, p38 of Buckland et
al (2001)):
density = [f(0)/2] x [n/L]

The first bit encompasses the estimation of the detection function.  It
is the second bit that is defined as the 'encounter rate' (number of
detections per amount of effort exerted; for line transects this is
measured in length of line travelled).  If you provide lengths only for
transects on which birds are detected, you'll overestimate this
encounter rate, and hence overestimate density.

Therefore, you must include transects (and their length) with no
detections.  If you look at the 'Stratify example.dst' in the Sample
Projects directory, you'll see that no objects were detected on
transects labelled 5, 6, 9, 10, 11,12, and 23.  That is how your project
ought to look.

messages.body_plain:
I communicated with Eric offlist.  The answer to his question is that it
is not valid to sum limits of confidence intervals.  The limits for a
sum is not the sum of the limits!  In his case he used a common
detection function which meant his stratum-specific estimates were
positively correlated which resulted in limits for the sum that were
greater than the sum of the limits.  The correct way to construct
confidence intervals for a sum is to construct the variance for the sum
and then compute the limits from that variance.  The variance of a sum
of independent variables is the sum of the variances but the limits for
the sum will be less than the sum of the limits.  Do not add confidence
limits and expect that it is meaningful!  --jeff

messages.body_plain:
Alex:

There's not quite enough information in your question to find the

solution, but I've followed this logic to think about your problem:

If your study area is 5.3ha, I'll pretend it is square, so that would

make it 230m on a side.  If you placed 9 transects into that site, I'll

pretend that you placed them systematically running north-to-south.  If

they are equally spaced, then they will need to be spaced roughly 29m

apart (9 transects have 8 spaces between them; 8 goes into 230 28.75 times).

I'm using the density estimation approach that uses effective strip

half-width (ESW, or mu); this is eqn 1.3 on p.5 of Buckland et al.

(2001).  D=n/(2.mu.L)

 From the information you provided, n=44, L=2250m, and A=5.3ha.  It is
information about the detection function that lets us estimate mu, so
I'm going to guess about mu.  If I guess that mu=10m (meaning that you
effectively see as many possums at perpendicular distances beyond 100m
as you missed at distances less than mu), then I get a density estimate
of 44/(2.10m.2250m)=44/45,000m^2.  Converting m^2 to ha, we get
44animals in 4.5ha or about 10 animal per hectare (within the covered
region of your sampling).  Scaling that up to the 5.3ha study area, we
estimate the number of animals to be 10 x 5.3 or 53 animals in the study

area.

The bigger the estimate of mu, the smaller the estimate of density.  So,

you'll get your estimate of abundance (25) if your estimated effective

strip half-width is about 20.7m.  Was that your estimate of ESW (shown

in your Distance output)?

This brings me back to my guess about your design.  If your transects

were placed something like 29m apart, and the estimated strip half-width

was 20.7m, then the area effectively sampled by your consecutive

transects would overlap (20.7m to the right of the left transect and

20.7m to the left of the right transect being greater than the

inter-transect separation).  That suggests that the covered region (the

area your sampling covered) exceeded the size of the study area.  This

can result in the paradox you observed in your analysis.

How many of my guesses were incorrect?
